name: Audio-Visual Systems
title: Audio-Visual Systems
answer: Audio-visual systems in interactive and experiential art are installations and performances where sound and moving image respond to each other, to the space, or to audience input in real time. They range from generative projections mapped onto architecture to sensor driven soundscapes and live cinema. The field sits at the intersection of media art, performance, and computational design, and it treats the machine as a co-performer rather than a fixed playback device.

sections.body: Audio-visual systems in interactive and experiential art are installations and performances where sound and moving image respond to each other, to the space, or to audience input in real time. They range from generative projections mapped onto architecture to sensor driven soundscapes and live cinema. The field sits at the intersection of media art, performance, and computational design, and it treats the machine as a co-performer rather than a fixed playback device.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run on a single workstation or a small cluster of computers with a dedicated graphics processing unit for real time rendering and a low latency audio interface for sound output. Common setups pair a visual engine with an audio engine, connected by a local protocol such as Open Sound Control, and use projectors, LED panels, loudspeakers, cameras, and depth sensors as the physical interface. Reliable power, cooling, and network isolation are often more important than raw compute, because a dropped frame or audio glitch breaks the experience.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is usually built by patching together modular components for signal analysis, synthesis, and mapping rather than training a single end to end model. An artist may use a camera or microphone to extract features such as motion, brightness, pitch, or onset, then map those features to parameters of a visual shader or a spatial audio field. The mapping is often deliberately loose or nonlinear so that the system feels alive, and the piece is tuned through repeated rehearsal in the actual exhibition space.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this field concentrate on three areas: the provenance of training data or sample libraries, the status of a live system as an original work, and the safety of physical installations. If a generative model is used, the artist should document which datasets or pretrained models were involved and whether their licenses permit public performance. Audience data from cameras or microphones raises privacy questions, and any installation with projection, strobe, or loud sound needs clear warnings and fail-safe controls. Provenance is also a curatorial concern, because a work that changes on every run may need a recorded score or system diagram to be preserved and restaged.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward tighter integration of real time machine learning with spatial computing, so that installations can understand gesture, gaze, and room acoustics without wearable sensors. Smaller on device models are making multi channel audio and high resolution projection more portable, while remote and networked performances are testing how a shared audio-visual space can work across latency. The main open question is not technical power but legibility: how much of the system's behaviour should be visible to an audience, and how an artist can keep authorship clear when the machine improvises.
